a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT — Standard practice tracks glucose concentration at the working electrode via electrochemical signal magnitude. My observable is the electrochemical impedance phase shift at the electrode-electrolyte interface, which directly correlates with the increasing insulating barrier of protein encapsulation before signal attenuation occurs.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing relation is the Randles circuit model: phase shift φ = arctan(ωRC), where ω is angular frequency, R is charge transfer resistance, and C is double-layer capacitance. As proteins encapsulate, R increases, causing measurable phase shift increase before glucose signal drop. For a typical sensor, a 5° phase shift increase corresponds to ~20% signal attenuation threshold.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components: Existing potentiostat circuit with added phase detection capability (off-the-shelf AD8302 phase detector), microcontroller (existing MCU), firmware update (no new hardware). Materials: Standard electrode materials, existing encapsulation. Procedure: Apply small-amplitude AC excitation (10 mV, 1 kHz) alongside DC measurement, calculate phase shift continuously between excitation and response signals. Development required: Firmware modification only.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — Installability: Same (no new sensors). Operability: Same (continuous monitoring, no user intervention). Maintenance: Same (no additional maintenance). Cost class: Same (phase detection circuit is <$0.50 in volume). Expected conclusion: Identical deployment burden with earlier detection of failure precursor.

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Implant 10 sensors in subcutaneous tissue of test subjects, monitor continuously for 14 days. Instruments: Reference blood glucose meter, data acquisition system. Pass/fail threshold: Phase shift increase <3° over 14 days maintains MARD <10%. Duration: 14 days. Kill criterion: If any sensor shows phase shift increase ≥3° before day 14, the approach fails.
